Early forms followed the bassoon, with a boot joint and a crook, some tone holes drilled obliquely; later it took a scaled-up cor anglais design. In 1889 the French maker Lorée redesigned it and brought it out under its French name, to extend the oboe family downwards. When the name reached Britain, composers mostly called it the bass oboe. In the early twentieth century it was often confused with the heckelphone, which has a similar range, and some works are ambiguously scored; afterwards it was made only sporadically by makers such as Lorée, mostly to order.

Its range is lower, sounding an octave below the written pitch, and it holds a distinctive place in the tenor-baritone region of the woodwinds. Its resonance is centred in the chest, which gives the tone a vocal warmth. Against the cor anglais it is fuller and rounder; against the treble oboe it has an added quiet and inward quality. This combination lets it fill a gap in range in chamber music and wind ensembles, with a result that is both warm and expressive.

The baritone oboe (Baritone oboe, also called the bass oboe) is a double-reed aerophone of the European woodwind family, Hornbostel–Sachs 422.112-71. Its tube is about twice as long as the C oboe's, it uses a larger double reed and a question-mark-shaped crook, it is written in treble clef and sounds an octave lower, with a lowest note of B2, and some models can take an extension to B♭2. It is played much like the oboe, held by hand or fixed with a sling, and it appears in orchestral, chamber and solo works.
